question: Tell me about a time you received feedback that your communication was unclear. What did you do about it?

raiseTranscript.text: My manager said a status update email I sent about a bug fix was missing the root cause and next steps, so the team had to ask follow-ups in the channel.
What exactly did you change after that?
I started writing the update in a doc first with sections for problem, cause, fix, and impact, then copied it into email. My next two updates got no questions.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you received feedback that your communication was unclear. What did you do about it?
Situation: manager flagged unclear bug status email
Action: added structured sections (problem/cause/fix/impact) in a doc before sending
Outcome: next updates needed no follow-up questions
Quote: "I started writing the update in a doc first with sections..."
Follow-up: Asked what changed; candidate described repeatable template
junior.raiseFeedback: The candidate described a concrete instance of unclear status communication and the direct change they made to structure. They showed they could apply the feedback immediately on their own work. This meets the bar for a junior role where the expectation is local ownership and quick iteration on individual output.

lowerTranscript.text: I got told my updates were hard to follow once. I tried to add more detail after that.
Can you give an example of what you added or how you checked if it helped?
I just wrote longer emails and hoped it was clearer. The manager didn't say anything else so I think it was fine.

lowerNotes: Q: same
Situation: vague mention of feedback on updates
Action: "wrote longer emails"
Outcome: assumed it was fine because no further comment
Quote: "I just wrote longer emails and hoped it was clearer"
Follow-up: Probing for specific change or verification yielded no evidence of iteration
junior.lowerFeedback: The story lacks a specific example of what was unclear and shows no structured attempt to improve or verify the change. The candidate treated the feedback as a one-time event rather than an opportunity to adjust their process. This lowers the bar for junior because even at this level we expect candidates to demonstrate they can act on direct feedback about their own work.

raiseTranscript.text: Two teams were misaligned on a shared API change because my design doc buried the breaking change in a long paragraph. A peer called it out in review.
How did you address it beyond that doc?

I rewrote the doc with a one-page summary and explicit callouts, then scheduled a 20-minute sync with both teams to walk through the impact. After that I started adding a "cross-team impact" section to every design doc I wrote.

raiseNotes: Q: same
Situation: buried breaking change in design doc caused cross-team misalignment
Action: rewrote with summary + callouts, ran sync, added reusable "cross-team impact" section to future docs
Outcome: clearer alignment on subsequent changes
Quote: "I started adding a cross-team impact section to every design doc"
Follow-up: Confirmed the change became a repeatable practice
senior.raiseFeedback: Candidate owned a cross-team communication failure, made the doc clearer, and turned the fix into a reusable practice that influenced how they wrote future docs. This raises the bar for senior because it shows both immediate correction and influence on their own output that others could adopt.

lowerTranscript.text: A design doc I wrote was called unclear by another team. I updated that one doc and moved on.
Did you change how you wrote later docs or help anyone else?
Not really, I just made sure that particular doc was fixed. The other team was happy after the update.

lowerNotes: Q: same
Situation: unclear design doc flagged by another team
Action: updated only that doc
Outcome: local fix, no broader change
Quote: "I updated that one doc and moved on"
Follow-up: No evidence of pattern change or influence beyond the single instance
senior.lowerFeedback: The candidate fixed the immediate artifact but showed no evidence of changing their approach for future work or helping the broader team avoid similar issues. At senior level we look for the feedback to produce a repeatable improvement that extends beyond one document; this story stays purely local and therefore lowers the bar.

raiseTranscript.text: Two of my engineers were sending updates that their peers found vague. I received the feedback in a skip-level.
What did you do with your team?

I ran a 30-minute workshop on writing updates with before/after examples from our own work, then required every engineer to have their next update reviewed by a peer before sending. Three months later the skip-level feedback on communication dropped to zero.

raiseNotes: Q: same
Situation: skip-level feedback that engineers' updates were unclear
Action: ran workshop with real examples, added peer review step for updates
Outcome: skip-level complaints on communication went to zero in three months
Quote: "I ran a 30-minute workshop on writing updates with before/after examples"
Follow-up: Tied action to measurable reduction in complaints
manager.raiseFeedback: The manager turned individual feedback into a team-level intervention with a clear mechanism (workshop + peer review) and tracked the result. This raises the bar for manager because it demonstrates developing the team's communication capability rather than just fixing one instance.

lowerTranscript.text: I told the engineers who were mentioned to be more careful with their updates.
Did you create any team process or check whether it improved?
I mentioned it in one-on-ones but didn't track it further. The complaints stopped after a while.

lowerNotes: Q: same
Situation: feedback on engineers' unclear updates
Action: told individuals to be more careful
Outcome: assumed improvement because complaints eventually stopped
Quote: "I told the engineers who were mentioned to be more careful"
Follow-up: No team process or measurement put in place
manager.lowerFeedback: The response stayed at the level of individual coaching without creating any scalable team practice or measurement. At manager level we expect the leader to build repeatable mechanisms that raise the whole team's standard; this story shows neither, so it lowers the bar.

raiseTranscript.text: After a reorg, multiple directors told me that strategy updates from my org were being interpreted differently across divisions, creating duplicate work.
How did you address it at org scale?

I created a single narrative template with required sections for intent, trade-offs, and owner, required every VP to use it for quarterly updates, and had my chief of staff run a monthly review of three random updates. Within two quarters the duplicate-work tickets dropped 40%.

raiseNotes: Q: same
Situation: post-reorg strategy updates causing cross-division misalignment
Action: introduced required narrative template, monthly audit by chief of staff
Outcome: 40% drop in duplicate-work tickets in two quarters
Quote: "I created a single narrative template with required sections for intent, trade-offs, and owner"
Follow-up: Showed org-level mechanism and quantified result
exec.raiseFeedback: The executive identified an org-wide communication failure, implemented a structural change (template + audit), and measured business impact. This raises the bar for exec because it demonstrates strategic judgment in turning ambiguous feedback into a scalable process that affected multiple teams and produced a clear metric.

lowerTranscript.text: I sent a note to my VPs asking them to make their updates clearer.
What process or measurement did you put in place?
I left it to each VP to handle. I didn't have bandwidth to track it centrally.

lowerNotes: Q: same
Situation: cross-division misalignment on strategy updates
Action: sent note to VPs
Outcome: delegated without follow-up or measurement
Quote: "I left it to each VP to handle"
Follow-up: No org-level mechanism or result tracking
exec.lowerFeedback: The candidate delegated the problem without creating any org-level mechanism or visibility. At exec level we expect the leader to own the system that produces clear communication across boundaries; this response shows neither ownership nor leverage and therefore lowers the bar.
